readerTitle: When three good businesses are worth less together
caseNote: 가상 사례 (호텔·아이스크림·렌터카 그룹, 카페 체인, 사내 전략팀) + 실제 연구 (Berger & Ofek, Khanna & Palepu, Campa & Kedia, Villalonga) + 실제 기업 (Berkshire Hathaway)
insight: 서로 무관한 사업을 묶는 일이 가치를 만들려면, 본사가 각 사업이 혼자서는 얻지 못하는 무언가(자본, 경영, 신뢰)를 줘야 한다.
misconception: 무관한 사업을 여러 개 가지면 위험이 분산되니 회사가 더 안전하고 더 가치 있어진다.

sources.text: Berger, P. G., & Ofek, E. (1995). Diversification's effect on firm value. Journal of Financial Economics, 37(1).
Khanna, T., & Palepu, K. (1997). Why focused strategies may be wrong for emerging markets. Harvard Business Review.
Campa, J. M., & Kedia, S. (2002). Explaining the diversification discount. Journal of Finance, 57(4).
Villalonga, B. (2004). Diversification discount or premium? New evidence from the business information tracking series. Journal of Finance, 59(2).
Berkshire Hathaway annual reports and shareholder letters (business lines, decentralized management)

factChecks.note: 가상 그룹 계산: 호텔 $40M + 아이스크림 $25M + 렌터카 $15M = $80M. 그룹 시가 $70M. 차이 $10M, $10M ÷ $80M = 12.5%.
Berger & Ofek(1995)가 보고한 평균 가치 손실 폭(약 13~15%)을 원문에서 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "roughly 13–15%"로 적었습니다.
Khanna & Palepu(1997)의 주장(제도가 약한 신흥시장에서는 사업그룹이 자본·인재·신뢰의 빈틈을 메울 수 있다)과 인도·한국 예시가 원문과 맞는지 확인하세요.
Campa & Kedia(2002), Villalonga(2004)는 다각화 기업이 다각화 이전부터 낮게 평가됐을 수 있어 할인의 상당 부분이 선택 효과일 수 있다고 주장합니다. 요약이 정확한지 확인하세요.
Berkshire Hathaway의 사업 구성(보험, 철도, 에너지, 소비재 브랜드)과 자회사 경영 자율 방침은 최신 연차보고서로 확인하세요.

cards.title: When three good businesses are worth less together
body: A group owns a hotel chain, an ice cream maker and a car rental firm. Each one is healthy.
Valued one by one, they'd be worth $80 million. Investors value the whole group at $70 million. Somewhere, $10 million went missing.

image.label: Three puzzle pieces that don't quite fit together
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 호텔 건물, 아이스크림 콘, 자동차 모양의 퍼즐 조각 세 개가 억지로 맞춰져 있고 틈이 벌어져 있음. 틈 사이로 동전이 새어 나옴. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Should your café chain buy a ski rental shop?
body: You run six cafés in a beach town. Summers are packed, winters are slow. An advisor suggests buying a ski rental business two hours away to balance the year.
What's the strongest reason to say yes?

options.text: Smoother yearly profits will make the company safer and worth more
options.feedback: Smoother income helps an owner whose savings are all in one business. But neither business earns a cent more because they share an owner.

options.text: You can run it better than its current owners, or fund it more cheaply
options.feedback: This is the only reason that adds value rather than just reshuffling it. If you can't name what you bring, the price is all you get.

options.text: It's on sale at a good price
options.feedback: A low price may reflect real problems. And a bargain you don't know how to run can cost more than it saves.

cards.title: Where did $10 million go?
body: The gap is 12.5% of the parts' value. Investors are saying the group, as run today, is worth less than its pieces would be on their own.

cards.title: Conglomerates
body: A **conglomerate** is one company that owns several businesses with little in common. They don't share kitchens, customers or suppliers.
So the parent can't add value by combining operations. It can only add value through money and management: deciding where cash goes, picking leaders, lending its name.
When investors doubt the parent adds enough, they apply a **conglomerate discount**, like the $10 million gap.

image.label: A head office linked to three unrelated businesses
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 위에 'Head office' 건물 하나, 아래에 호텔·공장·자동차 아이콘 세 개. 위아래로는 'Cash'와 'Managers' 화살표만 오가고, 세 사업 사이에는 연결선이 없음.

cards.title: Investors often see a discount.
body: In a 1995 study of US firms, Philip Berger and Eli Ofek found diversified companies were valued roughly 13–15% below what similar focused firms suggested. Common explanations:
list: **Investors can diversify themselves:** buying three separate shares is cheap
**Head office costs:** a layer that makes nothing
**Cross-subsidies:** a strong unit's cash props up a weak one
**Harder to judge:** outsiders struggle to value a mix

cards.title: Some parents earn their place.
body: Tarun Khanna and Krishna Palepu argued in 1997 that in markets where loans, skilled managers and trust are scarce, business groups in places like India and South Korea can fill those gaps for their units.
Berkshire Hathaway owns insurers, a railway, energy firms and consumer brands. It mostly leaves managers alone and focuses on where to put cash.
In both cases, the parent supplies something the units couldn't easily get alone.

cards.title: The discount is an average, not a law.
body: Later studies, such as Campa and Kedia (2002) and Villalonga (2004), suggest firms that diversify were often valued lower *before* they diversified. So owning many businesses may not cause all of the gap.
And a parent's edge lives in people. A group that thrives under one capital allocator can lose it when that person leaves.

cards.title: Your CEO wants to buy a software company.
body: You lead the strategy team at a mid-sized maker of industrial pumps. The CEO wants to use spare cash to buy a fast-growing app for booking fitness classes.
What should your team ask first?

options.text: Will it spread our risk beyond pumps?
options.feedback: Your shareholders can buy a fitness app stock themselves at no premium. Spreading risk alone doesn't justify paying for control.

options.text: What can we give this app that it can't get on its own?
options.feedback: If the answer is nothing, you're paying a premium for growth others can buy cheaper. If it's real, you have a case.

options.text: Is it growing faster than we are?
options.feedback: Growth matters, but the seller knows it too and prices it in. Buying growth at full price adds nothing.

cards.title: Owning unrelated businesses only pays if the owner adds something.
body: Spreading risk isn't enough. Name what the parent gives each business that it couldn't get alone.
**Try it today:** list each unit, product line or side business you run. Next to each, write one thing it gets from being yours. Note any blank lines.
